search_lead.cognate: OIr. dé 'gods' (gen. pl. dee) < *deywos ~ Ved. devá-; OIr. andé (an- privative + dé) ~ Ved. á-deva- < *n̥-deywo-: a polar pair 'god : un-god' built of the same stem and the same privative in both branches
search_lead.argument: In TBC (anchor) 'bendacht dee ⁊ andee fort' is a blessing from the whole class of beings, glossed by the text itself as the áes cumachta and the áes trebaire, i.e. a totality merism. RV 6.22.11c 'ná ... ádevaḥ várate ná deváḥ' ('neither un-god nor god obstructs') uses the same polar pair of devá- and its privative as a totality expression ('no one at all'). Same morphology (positive + n̥-privative of *deywo-), same figure (polar totality merism). Caveats: in the RV ádeva- usually means 'godless, impious' (of men/demons), and the RV slot is negated, not a blessing; privative polar pairs are a productive figure, so independent creation is possible. The Irish exegesis (andé = farmers) looks secondary learned glossing.

search_lead.cognate: OIr. muir ~ Lat. mare < *móri; OIr. tír ~ Lat. terra (both from *ters- 'dry')
search_lead.argument: Lóegaire's elemental guarantee (grían ⁊ éscae, uisce ⁊ áer, lá ⁊ adaig, muir ⁊ tír) is a catalogue of cosmic elements in pairs; Latin has the same cognate pair sea/land as a merism (terra marique) and Lucretius lists terra, sol, luna, mare together as the parts of the world. Only the sea/land pair is cognate (grían/sol, éscae/luna are not), the Latin context is cosmological, not an oath, and 'sea and land' is a near-universal merism; the Irish sea/land hits are overwhelmingly late annalistic 'do mhuir ⁊ do thír'. Weak: worth a reviewer's look only as an Italo-Celtic cognate merism. Elemental oaths with sun, earth, rivers as witnesses (Il. 3.276-280) are recalled, not cognate.

near_miss.lead: rest day and night: ON hvílði þann dag allan ok nóttina ~ Lat. nec noctu nec diu quietus (hvíla ~ quies < *kʷyeh₁-)
near_miss.why_not: Verb root is cognate, but day/night merism is universal, dagr/dies not cognate, and the contexts differ (Þorgeirr's silent meditation under the cloak vs a slave's complaint of toil); generic.
